title: Quiz: Search Strategies and Numerical Optimisation

questions.text: A grid search uses 50 points per parameter across 3 parameters. How many loss evaluations are needed?
questions.explanation: Grid search is O(nᵏ) where n = points per parameter and k = number of parameters. 50³ = 125,000 evaluations. This grows exponentially — with 10 parameters at 50 points each, you would need 50¹⁰ ≈ 10¹⁷ evaluations, which is computationally infeasible.

questions.text: In gradient descent, the learning rate α controls the size of the step taken in the direction of the gradient.
questions.explanation: The update rule is β ← β − α∇L(β). A large α means large steps (fast convergence but risk of overshooting the minimum). A small α means small steps (slow but stable). Choosing α well is one of the key challenges in gradient descent.

questions.text: optim() with method = 'BFGS' returns convergence = 1. What should you do?
options: Accept the result — convergence = 1 means success
Investigate: convergence ≠ 0 indicates failure; try different starting values or a different method
Increase the number of random starts
questions.explanation: In R's optim(), convergence = 0 means success. Any other code indicates a problem: the algorithm did not converge within the iteration limit, or it hit a boundary. The fix is usually to try different starting values, relax convergence tolerances, or use a different method.

questions.text: Why is lm() faster and more accurate than optim() for ordinary linear regression?
options: lm() uses a faster computer chip
lm() uses the closed-form OLS solution via QR decomposition — one matrix computation, no iteration
lm() uses gradient descent with a very large learning rate
lm() fits the model on a subset of the data
questions.explanation: OLS has the closed-form solution β̂ = (X'X)⁻¹X'y. lm() computes this via QR decomposition in a single pass — no iterations, no starting values, no convergence to check. optim() iterates, so it is always slower and subject to numerical approximation errors.

questions.text: When should you use optim() instead of lm() for fitting a regression-like model?
options: When the dataset has more than 1,000 rows
When the loss function is non-standard (e.g., MAE, a custom business loss, or a non-linear model)
When you want more accurate estimates than lm() provides
questions.explanation: lm() is specifically designed for minimising RSS (squared error). If you need to minimise a different loss — MAE, a weighted loss, a penalised likelihood, or the loss of a non-linear model — there is no closed-form solution and optim() (or specialised functions like rlm(), glm(), nls()) becomes necessary.

questions.text: Grid search always finds the exact global minimum of the loss function.
questions.explanation: Grid search only evaluates the loss at a finite set of pre-specified points. The true minimum may lie between grid points. Finer grids get closer to the true minimum but at quadratic cost. The closed-form OLS solution and gradient-based methods can find the true minimum exactly or to arbitrary precision.
